title: A 3D PINN-Based Framework for Patient-Specific Pulmonary Hemodynamics Using Windkessel Models
authors: Celia Taboada, Luis Nuñez, Angélica Casero, Pedro Navas
abstract: Cardiovascular fluid dynamics modeling relies heavily on mesh-based numerical methods such as Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD). While accurate, these methods entail significant computational costs and complex meshing workflows that limit their translation to clinical practice. Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) are a promising meshless alternative that embeds the governing equations directly into neural network training. In this work, we propose a PINN framework for pulsatile blood flow in patient-specific geometries with dynamic lumped-parameter Windkessel (RCR) outlet conditions representing distal vascular impedance. Coupling the Windkessel ODE to a 3D network raises two difficulties: the ODE alone does not fix the pressure level, and the local pressure variations that drive the flow are orders of magnitude smaller than the basal pressure imposed by the outlet. We address them by decomposing pressure into a time-dependent basal part and a spatially varying part, an initial condition and gauge for the Windkessel equation, a global mass-balance constraint, and a periodic Fourier embedding of time. Validated on 2D canonical channels (steady and pulsatile, with and without RCR outlet), the framework is then applied to a patient-specific right pulmonary artery, reproducing outlet flow, mean pressure, and the velocity and dynamic pressure fields with errors on the order of the data resolution. Finally, we solve the inverse problem of identifying the three Windkessel parameters of the outlet from synthetic data, recovering them with errors of about 0.3% from deliberately wrong initial values. Residual biases in the local pressure field and the need to test robustness to noisy clinical data remain open, but the results support PINNs as complementary tools for meshless hemodynamics and patient-specific digital twins.

infographic.key_insight: A 3D physics-informed neural network couples patient-specific pulmonary blood flow with Windkessel outlet dynamics by separating basal pressure from local pressure variations.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework supports meshless pulmonary hemodynamics modeling and outlet-parameter estimation toward patient-specific cardiovascular digital twins.
method: Embed flow equations and dynamic Windkessel (RCR) outlet conditions into PINN training.
Separate basal and spatial pressure; impose a Windkessel initial condition, pressure gauge, and global mass balance.
Use periodic Fourier time embedding to represent pulsatile flow.
infographic.evidence_signal: Tests on 2D channels and a patient-specific right pulmonary artery reproduced flow and pressure with errors on the order of data resolution; inverse estimation recovered three Windkessel parameters from synthetic data with about 0.3% error.
infographic.watch_item: Local pressure biases persist, and robustness to noisy clinical data remains untested.
infographic.paper_title: A 3D PINN-Based Framework for Patient-Specific Pulmonary Hemodynamics Using Windkessel Models

title: Measuring and Improving Transfer of Neural Surrogates for Vehicle Aerodynamics
authors: Favour Nerrise, Julian Busch, Gurpreet Singh Hora, Martin Sipka, Danielle C. Maddix, Georgia Olympia Brikis
abstract: Neural surrogates for external vehicle aerodynamics are fast alternatives to physics-based computational fluid dynamics (CFD) simulations. Their foundational limitation is a lack of zero-shot generalization across vehicle classes, which results in an expensive, custom training campaign for each new vehicle design. Similar to pretrained models in other fields, a pretrained surrogate should adapt to a new vehicle class using only a few simulations and stay accurate on its pretraining domain. No prior study has systematically tested this transfer behavior. We conduct a large-scale, controlled benchmarking study on five DrivAerML-pretrained surrogates across four independent target datasets. These datasets differ from the source in geometry, CFD solver, turbulence model, and flow conditions. We find that fine-tuning these surrogates outperforms training from scratch in fewer than half of the comparisons and lowers the accuracy of the surrogate on its source dataset. We introduce GeoReplay, a geometry- and gradient-aligned source replay that keeps source simulations resembling the target in training and applies their updates only when they agree with the target gradient. A risk bound separates geometric coverage from differences in the simulated physics, and we prove that every sufficiently small GeoReplay step decreases the target training objective. GeoReplay lowers the source error of fine-tuning in 77 of 80 settings and matches its target accuracy.

infographic.key_insight: Pretrained vehicle-aerodynamics surrogates transfer unreliably, while GeoReplay preserves source-domain accuracy without sacrificing fine-tuning’s target accuracy.
infographic.engineering_relevance: GeoReplay could help reuse aerodynamic surrogates across vehicle classes while limiting accuracy loss on previously modeled designs.
method: Benchmark five DrivAerML-pretrained surrogates on four independent target datasets.
Replay source simulations with geometries resembling the target vehicles.
Apply replay updates only when aligned with the target gradient.
infographic.evidence_signal: Fine-tuning beat training from scratch in fewer than half of comparisons; GeoReplay reduced source error relative to fine-tuning in 77 of 80 settings while matching target accuracy.
infographic.watch_item: GeoReplay requires retained source simulations, and its guarantee concerns sufficiently small steps on the target training objective—not unseen-target accuracy.
infographic.paper_title: Measuring and Improving Transfer of Neural Surrogates for Vehicle Aerodynamics

title: Nonlinearly Causal General-Relativistic Superfluid Hydrodynamics: Simulating Vortex Dynamics in Neutron-Star Interiors
authors: Yuan Feng, Elias R. Most, Lorenzo Gavassino
abstract: Neutron stars provide a natural laboratory for superfluid matter under extreme conditions. Its nonlinear dynamics is central to pulsar glitches, their possible links to fast radio bursts, and tidal interactions in inspiralling binaries. We develop a general-relativistic superfluid hydrodynamics framework incorporating entrainment, vortex forces, and line energy, and derive, for the first time, necessary and sufficient conditions for nonlinear causality and strong hyperbolicity. We also show that commonly used dissipative, force-balanced formulations without line tension are generically ill-posed at short wavelengths because of the Donnelly-Glaberson instability. Exploiting the analogy between vortex arrays with tension and force-free electrodynamics, we recast vortex dynamics in terms of effective electric and magnetic fields and drift velocities. This motivates a new finite-volume scheme combining constrained transport of superfluid vorticity with implicit electric-field evolution, enabling stable numerical evolution of the full system. We validate the scheme using an exact solution to the relativistic superfluid Riemann problem and Kelvin-wave dispersion relations, among other tests. Finally, we simulate dynamical, global general-relativistic two-fluid neutron-star equilibria, validate their oscillation modes, and present the first simplified calculation of superfluid interior spin-down with prescribed vortex release and repinning. The resulting stationary state retains both a net twist in the vortex array and residual differential rotation of the superfluid. Our framework thus enables nonlinear numerical studies of general-relativistic superfluid dynamics in neutron-star interiors.

infographic.key_insight: A general-relativistic superfluid framework establishes necessary and sufficient conditions for nonlinear causality and strong hyperbolicity, enabling simulations of neutron-star vortex dynamics.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework supports stable computational studies of superfluid dynamics relevant to pulsar glitches and neutron-star tidal interactions.
method: Include entrainment, vortex forces, and vortex line energy in relativistic two-fluid hydrodynamics.
Express vortex dynamics through effective electric and magnetic fields using an analogy with force-free electrodynamics.
Combine finite-volume evolution with constrained transport of superfluid vorticity and implicit electric-field evolution.
infographic.evidence_signal: Validation includes an exact relativistic superfluid Riemann solution, Kelvin-wave dispersion relations, and oscillation modes of global relativistic two-fluid neutron-star equilibria.
infographic.watch_item: The spin-down demonstration prescribes vortex release and repinning, so its residual differential rotation and vortex twist require testing with more realistic unpinning physics.
infographic.paper_title: Nonlinearly Causal General-Relativistic Superfluid Hydrodynamics: Simulating Vortex Dynamics in Neutron-Star Interiors

title: Singular layer neural networks for the Navier-Stokes equations at small viscosity
authors: Teng-Yuan Chang, Gung-Min Gie, Youngjoon Hong, Chang-Yeol Jung
abstract: We develop neural network methods for the two-dimensional incompressible Navier-Stokes equations at a small viscosity $\varepsilon > 0$, whose accuracy is uniform in $\varepsilon$ and whose residual is evaluated on a grid that does not resolve the vorticity boundary layer. In the vorticity-stream function formulation with the slip boundary conditions, a vorticity layer of width $\sqrt{\varepsilon}$ forms along the walls. The trial function of the singular layer Physics-Informed Neural Network (sl-PINN) contains the corrector of the asymptotic analysis, together with the law that fixes its amplitude at the wall. The amplitude is tied to the wall trace of the network itself, so that the method requires no a priori knowledge of the limit solution. The sl-PINN keeps the error uniform in $\varepsilon$ over six decades, for the Stokes and the Navier-Stokes equations alike, although in the latter the wall trace travels with the flow and is not known in advance. An enrichment that uses the thin scale but leaves the profile and the amplitude of the layer free deteriorates as $\varepsilon\to0$. Since the corrector carries the layer analytically, the Laplacian in the residual can be discretized by a finite volume flux difference on a coarse grid. The resulting singular layer Finite Volume Neural Network (sl-FVNN) attains the same uniform accuracy as the sl-PINN, to within the scatter of the random seed, at about half the cost of a training step. The combination of the asymptotic corrector with the coarse-grid finite volume discretization is the main result of this article.

infographic.key_insight: Embedding an asymptotic boundary-layer corrector in neural trial functions preserves accuracy at small viscosity without requiring a grid that resolves the layer.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach could reduce training costs for low-viscosity flow simulations by representing thin near-wall vorticity layers analytically rather than through mesh refinement.
method: Build sl-PINN trial functions with a corrector for the √ε-wide vorticity layer.
Tie the corrector amplitude to the network’s wall trace, avoiding prior knowledge of the limit solution.
Use coarse-grid finite-volume Laplacian fluxes in sl-FVNN to reduce residual-evaluation cost.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports uniform accuracy over six viscosity decades for Stokes and Navier–Stokes tests, with sl-FVNN matching sl-PINN within random-seed scatter at about half the cost per training step.
infographic.watch_item: The reported results concern two-dimensional flows with slip boundary conditions; applicability to other boundary conditions or geometries remains to be established.
infographic.paper_title: Singular layer neural networks for the Navier-Stokes equations at small viscosity

title: Droplet formation dynamics in a T-junction via pulsed electrohydrodynamics
authors: He Yan, Kang luo, Bin Gong, Lei Wang
abstract: Numerical simulations based on the phase-field lattice Boltzmann method are employed to investigate droplet formation dynamics in a T-junction microchannel under pulsed electrohydrodynamics. The applied electric field modulates the interfacial morphology, thereby altering the hydrodynamic stress distribution acting on the liquid-liquid interface. Three configurations are examined: no electric field, top-biased electrode, and bottom-biased electrode. The results show that the top-biased electrode promotes rapid transverse migration of the dispersed phase towards the upper wall, thereby accelerating the transition to the channel-blocking stage. By contrast, under the bottom-biased electrode, the dispersed phase first adheres to the lower wall and subsequently deforms upward under the electric force. As a result, the droplet formation dynamics are strongly affected by the spatial distribution of the electric field. The droplet generation process is further divided into a filling stage and a squeezing stage based on theoretical analysis. During the filling stage, the electric force modifies the filling duration but has little influence on the filling flux. During the squeezing stage, the necking rate and breakup time are governed by the pinning of the dispersed-phase contact line on the channel wall. Compared with constant electric forcing, pulsed electric forcing introduces an additional temporal degree of freedom, enabling stage-dependent modulation of interfacial evolution and breakup dynamics. Finally, droplet sequence diagrams and regime maps are presented for different pulse parameters. The results demonstrate that pulsed electrohydrodynamics in a T-junction enables active and programmable control of consecutive droplet generation.

infographic.key_insight: Pulsed electric fields enable programmable droplet generation in a T-junction by controlling interface motion, wall contact, and breakup timing.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Electrode placement and pulse timing offer design controls for microfluidic systems requiring tunable, consecutive droplet production.
method: Simulate two-phase flow using the phase-field lattice Boltzmann method.
Compare no-field, top-biased, and bottom-biased electrode configurations.
Analyze filling and squeezing stages and map droplet regimes across pulse parameters.
infographic.evidence_signal: Simulations show electrode-dependent interface evolution, while droplet sequence diagrams and regime maps demonstrate sensitivity to pulse parameters.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract reports numerical results without experimental validation; practical performance may depend on accurately reproducing wall wetting and contact-line pinning.
infographic.paper_title: Droplet formation dynamics in a T-junction via pulsed electrohydrodynamics

title: Onset of three dimensionality in transonic shock boundary layer interaction over a natural laminar flow airfoil
authors: Abhijeet Guha, Aditi Sengupta
abstract: The development of three-dimensionality in transonic shock--boundary-layer interactions (SBLI) can significantly influence the aerodynamic response of natural laminar flow (NLF) airfoils, yet the associated vorticity dynamics remain insufficiently understood. The present study investigates the short-time evolution of transonic SBLI over the SHM1 NLF airfoil using high-fidelity three-dimensional (3D) simulations at three operating conditions reported by Fujino et al., Natural-laminar-flow airfoil development for a lightweight business jet, J. Aircraft 40, 609-615 (2003). The selected cases represent three distinct operating regimes: the initial development of a normal shock, drag divergence, and shock-induced separation. Comparisons with previously reported two-dimensional (2D) simulations establish the temporal interval over which the spanwise-averaged 3D flow remains close to the corresponding 2D evolution, while departures in surface pressure and skin-friction responses identify the subsequent development of 3D effects within the SBLI region. The temporal evolution of volume-integrated streamwise and wall-normal enstrophies further characterizes the development of the associated 3D vortical field. The compressible enstrophy transport equation (CETE) is subsequently employed to examine the mechanisms governing the evolution of the 3D vortical field. Viscous and compressibility-related terms dominate the normalized enstrophy budget during the early evolution, while vortex stretching remains a minor contribution in the normal-shock and drag-divergence regimes but becomes appreciable, albeit intermittently, with the development of shock-induced separation. Across the three operating regimes, the same principal enstrophy-transport mechanisms remain active, but their relative contributions to the normalized budget are redistributed with the SBLI topology.

infographic.key_insight: Early three-dimensional vorticity evolution in transonic shock–boundary-layer interactions is dominated by viscous and compressibility-related mechanisms, with vortex stretching becoming appreciable but intermittent during shock-induced separation.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Understanding when three-dimensional effects emerge can inform the use of two-dimensional simulations to assess natural-laminar-flow airfoil performance near transonic operating limits.
method: High-fidelity 3D simulations of the SHM1 airfoil across normal-shock development, drag divergence, and shock-induced separation.
Comparison of spanwise-averaged 3D surface pressure and skin friction with previously reported 2D simulations.
Streamwise and wall-normal enstrophy tracking and compressible enstrophy-transport budget analysis.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across three operating conditions, 2D–3D comparisons identify an initial agreement interval and subsequent departures, while normalized enstrophy budgets show regime-dependent redistribution among the same principal mechanisms.
infographic.watch_item: The study addresses short-time evolution on one airfoil; its findings do not establish long-time behavior or universal limits for 2D modeling.
infographic.paper_title: Onset of three dimensionality in transonic shock boundary layer interaction over a natural laminar flow airfoil

title: HAVAPlot: A Web-Based Scientific Visualization and Post-Processing Platform
authors: Ozgur Tumuklu
abstract: This paper presents HAVAPlot, a browser-based framework for scientific visualization and post-processing of numerical simulation data. Operating entirely within the user's browser, HAVAPlot requires no software installation or data uploads while supporting mesh-based and tabular datasets beyond computational fluid dynamics. The framework directly reads native OpenFOAM cases, including polyhedral meshes, ASCII and binary fields, boundary data, and Lagrangian particles, as well as legacy and XML VTK files and tabular datasets. It provides line, contour, and three-dimensional plots; exact polyhedral slicing; boundary extraction; variable calculations; customizable color scales; symmetry mirroring; zoomed insets; streamlines; isosurfaces; particle visualization; and vector PDF/EPS and data export. The underlying numerical algorithms are independently verified. Cell centers and volumes agree with an independent implementation of OpenFOAM's geometric algorithm, while 6.1 million field values across four two-dimensional, axisymmetric, and three-dimensional production cases are reproduced to machine precision. For analytical fields on distorted hexahedral meshes, cell-to-point interpolation exhibits second-order convergence in the interior and first-order convergence at boundaries. Meshes containing 250,000 cells load in at most 1.3 seconds. Applications to an impinging supersonic jet, hypersonic cylinder flow, a hybrid particle-continuum cold-spray nozzle, a three-dimensional gas-bearing film, and supersonic cone flow demonstrate the framework's capabilities.

infographic.key_insight: HAVAPlot enables browser-based scientific visualization and post-processing without software installation or simulation-data uploads.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Engineers can inspect native OpenFOAM, VTK, and tabular results locally and export publication-ready figures and processed data.
method: Read native OpenFOAM cases, including polyhedral meshes, binary fields, boundaries, and particles.
Generate exact polyhedral slices, contours, streamlines, isosurfaces, and particle visualizations.
Verify mesh geometry, field reading, and interpolation against independent implementations and analytical fields.
infographic.evidence_signal: Validation reproduced 6.1 million field values to machine precision across four production cases; interpolation converged at second order internally and first order at boundaries, while 250,000-cell meshes loaded within 1.3 seconds.
infographic.watch_item: Boundary interpolation is only first-order accurate, and browser performance on substantially larger meshes is not established by the abstract.
infographic.paper_title: HAVAPlot: A Web-Based Scientific Visualization and Post-Processing Platform

title: Stochastic Representation-Inspired Physics-Informed Neural Networks for Incompressible Fluid Flows
authors: Zihao Guo, Zhongmin Qian
abstract: The effectiveness of neural networks in solving partial differential equations depends not only on their approximation capability but also on the suitability of their representations for the underlying solutions. Motivated by stochastic integral representations of incompressible fluid flows and the associated Biot--Savart kernel, we propose a Biot--Savart-informed (i.e. physics-informed) neural network (BS-PINN) for the incompressible Navier--Stokes equations. By extracting a rational profile from a regularized Biot--Savart kernel, we construct a smooth activation function with fixed and learnable kernel scales. Both variants retain the conventional velocity--pressure formulation and physics-informed training framework, allowing the influence of the activation function to be examined independently. We evaluate the method on five benchmarks, including Kovasznay flow, cylinder wake, three-dimensional Beltrami flow, Taylor--Green vortex, and double shear layer. Across 21 benchmark--architecture comparisons, both variants consistently reduce the combined velocity error relative to the conventional $\tanh$-based PINN, achieving mean relative error reductions of 31.7\% and 33.2\%, respectively. Improvements are also observed in reported pressure and vorticity errors. Notably, the double-shear-layer experiments demonstrate improved resolution of localized shear structures and, for BS-PINN-F, qualitatively clearer vortex-roll-up patterns in the long-time simulation. These findings highlight the potential of incorporating analytical flow structures into neural-network representations for incompressible flow simulations.

infographic.key_insight: Biot–Savart-inspired activation functions improve incompressible-flow PINN accuracy without changing the conventional velocity–pressure formulation.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Flow-informed neural representations could improve simulations of wakes, vortices, and localized shear structures.
method: Extract a smooth rational activation profile from a regularized Biot–Savart kernel.
Test fixed-scale and learnable-scale activation variants.
Retain standard physics-informed training to isolate the activation’s influence.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across five flow benchmarks and 21 benchmark–architecture comparisons, fixed- and learnable-scale variants reduced combined velocity error versus tanh PINNs by averages of 31.7% and 33.2%, respectively.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not establish computational cost or generalization to high-Reynolds-number turbulent flows.
infographic.paper_title: Stochastic Representation-Inspired Physics-Informed Neural Networks for Incompressible Fluid Flows

title: Closed-loop policy optimisation for cylinder wake control via differentiable simulation
authors: Siwen Zhang, Xizeng Zhao, Zhouteng Ye, Yulin Xie, Zesheng Yao
abstract: Suppressing vortex shedding behind a circular cylinder is a classical problem in active flow control.Model-free deep reinforcement learning (DRL) learns such policies by interacting with the flow without differentiating its dynamics, which typically requires a large interaction budget. This study optimises closed-loop policies by differentiable simulation: control-loss gradients propagate through the simulated flow to the policy parameters, which are updated by reverse-mode automatic differentiation. The policy maps local velocity measurements to a jet amplitude imposed through differentiable synthetic-jet boundary conditions. In a two-dimensional confined cylinder wake at Rey=100, eight policy updates (about 78 shedding periods of forward simulation) give approximately 8% drag reduction and 99.6% suppression of lift fluctuations, the drag level being comparable to reported DRL results. Suppression is sustained by feedback: a mean-matched constant jet does not maintain it, whereas the same policy responds similarly at three activation phases and recovers after upstream disturbances. A velocity-deviation reward alone retains strong suppression, and observations of two instantaneous velocity components at one near-wake or surface location reach about 99.8% suppression, whereas a single surface pressure leaves residual oscillations. Together with related DRL results, this suggests that reward and observation requirements here are set by policy optimisation and flow physics.

infographic.key_insight: Differentiating through a cylinder-wake simulation enables closed-loop policies to achieve approximately 8% drag reduction and 99.6% suppression of lift fluctuations in eight policy updates.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Gradient-based feedback control offers a potentially interaction-efficient route to suppressing vortex shedding with local velocity sensing and synthetic-jet actuation.
method: Map local velocity measurements to synthetic-jet amplitude.
Backpropagate control-loss gradients through simulated flow and differentiable jet boundary conditions.
Update policy parameters using reverse-mode automatic differentiation.
infographic.evidence_signal: In a 2D confined wake at Re=100, training used about 78 shedding periods of forward simulation; tests showed consistent responses across three activation phases and recovery after upstream disturbances.
infographic.watch_item: Results are limited to a 2D confined flow at Re=100; transfer to turbulent 3D flows or physical hardware remains unestablished.
infographic.paper_title: Closed-loop policy optimisation for cylinder wake control via differentiable simulation

title: Effects of sinusoidal pitch amplitude and phase on power extraction and pitching-energy exchange in a single-blade vertical-axis turbine model
authors: Zihan Zhang, Anchi Li, Qimin Feng, Yuanhang Zhu, Qiang Zhong
abstract: Sinusoidal blade pitching can improve vertical-axis turbine performance, but whether a blade could follow the same motion passively depends on the energy exchanged through pitching. This study experimentally examines 480 prescribed-pitch conditions using a single-blade model following a circular trajectory in a water channel at four tip-speed ratios (TSRs) from 1.25 to 3.14. The amplitude associated with the highest measured power decreases from 16° to 12° and then 8° as TSR increases, with the corresponding phase shifting from 0 to pi/4. At TSRs of 1.25 and 3.14, the cycle-averaged power coefficient increases from 0.0047 to 0.1037 and from 0.4698 to 0.5948, respectively. Pitching-energy maps show nearly neutral net hydrodynamic pitching work for the highest-performing motions at the two lower TSRs and net energy transfer from the flow to pitching at the two higher TSRs. Virtual damping narrows the positive-energy region, although the higher-TSR best-tested motions retain an energy surplus at nonzero damping. However, net energy transfer from the flow to pitching also occurs for motions with substantial power losses. At the lowest TSR, phase-resolved force measurements and particle image velocimetry link the gain to delayed dynamic-stall-vortex formation and shedding, prolonged favorable loading, and reduced subsequent negative power. At the highest TSR, the flow and loading change locally, with little alteration of the main power-producing event. The joint maps identify performance-enhancing motions with an energetic margin against assumed dissipation, providing candidates for further passive or assisted pitching studies.

infographic.key_insight: Well-tuned sinusoidal pitching boosts turbine power, but net flow-to-pitch energy transfer alone does not guarantee improved performance.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Joint power and pitching-energy maps identify promising motions for passive or assisted blade-pitch designs with a margin against assumed dissipation.
method: Tested 480 prescribed-pitch conditions on a single blade moving along a circular path in a water channel.
Varied pitch amplitude and phase at four tip-speed ratios from 1.25 to 3.14.
Combined pitching-energy maps and virtual damping with phase-resolved force measurements and particle image velocimetry.
infographic.evidence_signal: At tip-speed ratios of 1.25 and 3.14, the best-tested pitching motions raised cycle-averaged power coefficients from 0.0047 to 0.1037 and from 0.4698 to 0.5948, respectively.
infographic.watch_item: Prescribed-pitch energy surpluses do not establish passive realizability; actual motion and performance depend on pitch dynamics and mechanical losses.
infographic.paper_title: Effects of sinusoidal pitch amplitude and phase on power extraction and pitching-energy exchange in a single-blade vertical-axis turbine model

title: $H_2$-optimal riblet profiles for turbulence suppression in channel flows
authors: Daniel W. Hartman, Armin Zare
abstract: The drag-reducing properties of streamwise-elongated surface corrugations, commonly referred to as riblets, have been extensively studied through experiments, simulations, and reduced-order modeling. Notably, the linearized Navier-Stokes framework introduced by Ran, Zare, and Jovanovic (J. Fluid Mech., vol. 906, 2021) employs volume penalization to model riblet-induced boundary conditions and predict drag reduction. These approaches typically quantify drag reduction as a function of a single geometric parameter, such as spanwise spacing or groove cross-sectional area, evaluated over fixed riblet shapes. As a result, identifying optimal riblet geometries across a broader design space often necessitates exhaustive parametric studies. To address this problem, we propose an optimization framework for the systematic design of optimal riblet shapes. Accordingly, we reformulate the volume penalization term in the linearized dynamics as a structured state-feedback operator. Targeting maximal suppression of turbulence, we pose a composite optimization problem that minimizes the steady-state variance of velocity fluctuations and riblet-induced dynamical augmentations while maintaining a constant bulk-flux. For a fixed spanwise wavelength (riblet spacing), this framework yields optimal wall-normal profiles that achieve maximal turbulence attenuation.

infographic.key_insight: The proposed H₂ optimization framework designs riblet wall-normal profiles to maximally attenuate turbulence at a fixed spanwise spacing.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Systematic riblet shape optimization could guide drag-reducing surface design without exhaustive searches over predefined geometries.
method: Model riblets through volume penalization in linearized Navier–Stokes dynamics.
Recast penalization as a structured state-feedback operator.
Minimize steady-state velocity-fluctuation variance and riblet-induced dynamical augmentations while maintaining constant bulk flux.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports optimal profiles for fixed riblet spacing but provides no quantitative attenuation results or experimental validation.
infographic.watch_item: Turbulence attenuation in the linearized model does not by itself establish drag reduction in fully nonlinear flows.
infographic.paper_title: $H_2$-optimal riblet profiles for turbulence suppression in channel flows

title: How Meandering Flow Sculpts Ice
authors: Yihong Du, Jin Hu, Feng Wang, Lars ten Hacken, Ziqi Wang, Rui Yang
abstract: Ice-water phase change subject to a mean flow widely exists in the Cryosphere, with implications on glacier evolution, human transportation, flooding events, etc. Understanding the relevant phase change dynamics requires identifying the roles of shear and rotation due to the mean flow. Combining experiments, numerical simulations and theoretical modelling, we reveal the combined effects of shear and rotation on the coupled dynamics of water flow, heat transfer and phase change in an annular system. Increasing shear and rotation drive a stronger secondary circulation which significantly enhances global heat transfer and redistributes the radial heat flux, and eventually lead to a thinner equilibrium ice layer and a larger ice thickness difference in the radial direction. Further, we develop an integral thermal balance model that explains the mean ice thickness through estimating the additional heat transfer, and a local thermal balance model that explains the inner-outer ice thickness difference by relating it to the non-uniform convective heat flux. The local model shows qualitative agreement with field measurements when applied to an ice-covered meandering river. These results contribute to understanding the common physical mechanism for ice-water phase change under shear and rotation, offering a theoretical basis for explaining and predicting ice evolution in meandering rivers among other relevant scenarios.

infographic.key_insight: Stronger shear and rotation intensify secondary circulation, enhancing heat transfer and producing thinner, more radially uneven equilibrium ice.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The findings could improve predictions of ice evolution in meandering rivers, informing flood-risk assessment and winter transportation planning.
method: Combine experiments, numerical simulations, and theory in an annular ice–water system.
Model mean ice thickness using an integral thermal balance.
Relate inner–outer thickness differences to nonuniform convective heat flux using a local thermal balance.
infographic.evidence_signal: Annular experiments and simulations support the proposed mechanism, while the local model shows qualitative agreement with field measurements from an ice-covered meandering river.
infographic.watch_item: Field agreement is qualitative; predictive accuracy in natural rivers with more complex geometry and thermal forcing remains to be established.
infographic.paper_title: How Meandering Flow Sculpts Ice

title: Augmentation of cardiovascular flow measurements with generative diffusion models
authors: Fabio Guglietta, Tianyi Li, Francesco Viola, Luca Biferale
abstract: Cardiovascular imaging offers several ways to measure blood flow, but each provides an incomplete, resolution-limited, or noisy view of the underlying dynamics. Reconstructing the missing information is inherently ambiguous because several flow fields may be compatible with the same observation. Here, we investigate generative diffusion models as tools for cardiovascular-flow generation and reconstruction using a fully controlled state-of-the-art dataset from a digital twin of a healthy human left heart. First, we show how unconditional samples reproduce the changing anatomy and the highly fluctuating statistical properties of the flow throughout the cardiac cycle. Second, we test the conditional inference of our generative model by reconstructing an entire 2D planar section of geometry and flow configurations from a limited portion. Repeated reconstructions allow us to represent a range of plausible completions, going beyond a single deterministic estimate, while their mean retains the principal features of the reference flow. Comparison with a Gaussian process regression baseline on the same reduced domain highlights the main advantage of diffusion models: their reconstructed ensembles capture a broader range of velocity and gradient fluctuations, better encompassing ground-truth features that the baseline distributions can miss. Our results provide a quantitative proof of concept for probabilistic reconstruction of incomplete cardiovascular-flow measurements and demonstrate the potential for groundbreaking applications to the augmentation of in-vivo cardiovascular imaging data.

infographic.key_insight: Generative diffusion models reconstruct missing cardiovascular flow information as ensembles of plausible fields rather than a single deterministic estimate.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Probabilistic flow reconstruction could augment incomplete cardiovascular imaging while representing ambiguity in unmeasured regions.
method: Train on a controlled digital-twin dataset of a healthy human left heart.
Generate unconditional samples of changing anatomy and flow across the cardiac cycle.
Reconstruct full 2D geometry and flow sections from partial observations, comparing ensembles with Gaussian process regression.
infographic.evidence_signal: On the digital-twin dataset, reconstruction means retained principal reference-flow features, while diffusion ensembles captured broader velocity and gradient fluctuations than the Gaussian process baseline.
infographic.watch_item: This proof of concept uses simulated healthy-heart data and 2D sections; performance on noisy in-vivo measurements and diseased anatomy remains unestablished.
infographic.paper_title: Augmentation of cardiovascular flow measurements with generative diffusion models

title: A sliding mode observer perspective on chaos synchronisation of turbulent flows
authors: Defne E. Ozan, Andrew Wynn
abstract: State estimation of turbulent flows is challenging as infinitesimal prediction errors grow exponentially due to chaos. However, when signals from one chaotic system (the master) are injected into an identical system with different initial conditions (the slave), the slave can synchronise with the master --- a phenomenon observed in turbulent flows. From a control-theoretic perspective, this synchronisation problem can be viewed as observer design. We first show that synchronisation by direct substitution of observed variables into the slave system is equivalent to a sliding mode observer. This perspective enables the analytical verification of stability as well as the design of feedback for robustness. We focus on reduced-order Navier--Stokes models with quadratic non-linearities, a broad class of systems for which stability can be analysed by seeking Lyapunov functions through parameter-dependent linear matrix inequalities solved via semidefinite programming. Extending this framework, we develop a neural network approach combining a neural ordinary differential equation with a decoder to learn data-driven mappings from observation histories to companion forms, where observer design is greatly simplified. Results are demonstrated on the Lorenz system and a nine-dimensional reduced order model of a turbulent shear flow. This work opens opportunities in the rigorous development of observers for turbulent flows.

infographic.key_insight: Synchronising chaotic flow models by directly substituting observed variables is equivalent to a sliding mode observer, enabling stability analysis and robustness-oriented feedback design.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This framework supports principled state estimation for reduced-order turbulent flows despite chaotic amplification of prediction errors.
method: Interpret master–slave synchronisation as sliding mode observer design.
Seek Lyapunov stability certificates using parameter-dependent linear matrix inequalities and semidefinite programming.
Combine a neural ODE and decoder to learn mappings from observation histories to companion forms that simplify observer design.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports demonstrations on the Lorenz system and a nine-dimensional reduced-order model of turbulent shear flow.
infographic.watch_item: Validation is limited to low-dimensional models; scalability and robustness to noisy measurements or model mismatch in full turbulent flows remain to be established.
infographic.paper_title: A sliding mode observer perspective on chaos synchronisation of turbulent flows

title: A curvature-corrected port-Hamiltonian reduced-order model for dissipative sloshing with contact-line hysteresis in low-gravity tanks
authors: Gianni Cassoni, Fabrizio Gennari, Jacopo Serafini, Pierangelo Masarati
abstract: A physics-based reduced-order model unifies curved-meniscus inertia, viscous losses and nonsmooth contact-line stick-slip in a passive port-Hamiltonian formulation for lateral sloshing in cylindrical tanks. Dirichlet-Neumann and Jacobi operators describe inertia and restoring forces, while a convex potential combines bulk, Stokes-layer and contact-line dissipation. Analytical propagation between stick-slip events supports faster-than-real-time simulation of coupled spacecraft translation and sloshing. The viscous closure agrees within 5% with a reference Stokes calculation, and the model reproduces the Henderson-Miles modal measurements and the Cocciaro hysteretic decay. Across 42 drop-tower and ground measurements, curvature correction reduces the root-mean-square frequency error from 24 to 4%. For flight and ground tests from the Middeck 0-Gravity Dynamics Experiment (MODE), frequency errors range from 0.9 to 7.1%, while ideal contact lines underestimate the damping ratios from the MODE fits by 38-87%. One hysteresis width, calibrated on the lowest orbital water excitation, predicts higher orbital excitations and the ground test with normalised force errors of 11-35%, against 149-208% for an ideal pinned line. It predicts 8.5% resonance softening against 7.3% measured, which the tested one-parameter damping laws miss. Uncertain wetting and remaining response discrepancies motivate damping ranges in spacecraft control analyses.

infographic.key_insight: A passive, physics-based sloshing surrogate combines curved-meniscus effects, viscous losses and contact-line hysteresis to improve low-gravity tank predictions.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Faster-than-real-time coupled spacecraft–sloshing simulation can support control analysis while accounting for uncertain damping.
method: Port-Hamiltonian reduced-order model with curvature-corrected inertia and restoring forces.
Convex dissipation potential combining bulk, Stokes-layer and contact-line losses.
Analytical propagation between nonsmooth contact-line stick–slip events.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across 42 drop-tower and ground measurements, curvature correction reduced RMS frequency error from 24% to 4%; MODE force errors were 11–35% with calibrated hysteresis versus 149–208% for an ideal pinned line.
infographic.watch_item: Uncertain wetting and remaining response discrepancies warrant damping ranges rather than a single nominal value in spacecraft control analyses.
infographic.paper_title: A curvature-corrected port-Hamiltonian reduced-order model for dissipative sloshing with contact-line hysteresis in low-gravity tanks

title: Theory of magneto-electrokinetics in unidirectional electrolyte flow: Hydrodynamic potential and Hall effect
authors: Yoav Tsori
abstract: We develop a theoretical framework for magneto-electrokinetic transport in dilute electrolytes under unidirectional flow and streaming current conditions. Unlike standard magnetohydrodynamics in liquid metals, where charge carriers are electrons and conductivity is typically uniform, electrolytes exhibit spatially varying ion densities and additional forces such as osmotic pressure. In steady state, the coupled Navier--Stokes, Nernst--Planck, and Poisson equations become analytically tractable. We derive a Boltzmann-like expression for ion distributions that incorporates both the electrostatic potential and a novel hydrodynamic potential arising from the magnetic field. This potential depends explicitly on the flow profile and is not screened close to the bounding walls. Applying the theory to Poiseuille flow, we derive expressions for the induced Hall potential and demonstrate its near-linear dependence on flow velocity and magnetic field strength, while remaining largely independent of salt concentration. To validate this one-dimensional framework, we analyze the two-dimensional spatial transients near the channel entrance. We demonstrate a separation of length scales: the Hall electric field and space charge adjust to the magnetic field almost instantaneously, whereas the macroscopic salt concentration wake develops over a much longer Graetz length dictated by the Péclet number. We also examine a similar flow with counterions only and no added salt, determining the resulting potential and ion distributions. This work offers new theoretical tools for understanding ion transport in microfluidic and electrochemical systems.

infographic.key_insight: A magnetic-field-induced hydrodynamic potential modifies ion distributions in flowing electrolytes, producing a Hall potential that is nearly linear in flow velocity and magnetic field strength but largely independent of salt concentration.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework can inform magnetic control and interpretation of ion transport in microfluidic and electrochemical systems.
method: Couple steady-state Navier–Stokes, Nernst–Planck, and Poisson equations for unidirectional electrolyte flow.
Derive ion distributions incorporating electrostatic and hydrodynamic potentials, then analyze Poiseuille flow and counterion-only conditions.
Examine two-dimensional entrance transients to distinguish rapid electrical adjustment from slower salt redistribution.
infographic.evidence_signal: Analytical results and entrance-region analysis support the predicted Hall response and separation of electrical and salt-transport length scales; the abstract reports no experimental validation.
infographic.watch_item: Applicability beyond dilute electrolytes and steady, unidirectional flow requires further validation.
infographic.paper_title: Theory of magneto-electrokinetics in unidirectional electrolyte flow: Hydrodynamic potential and Hall effect

title: Influence of an oxide cap on the combustion of aluminum particles using boundary-layer resolved simulations
authors: Hesheng Bao, Hongchao Chu, Shibam Bose, Heinz Pitsch
abstract: A distinctive feature of burning aluminum particles is the condensation of the primary combustion product, alumina, forming an oxide cap that covers part of the aluminum particle and alters the local combustion characteristics. This study systematically investigates the effects of an oxide cap on the combustion characteristics and interfacial processes of aluminum particles, using boundary-layer resolved simulations, considering variations in cap size, cap position relative to the flow direction, and the particle Reynolds number, $\mathrm{Re_p}$. The oxide cap modifies both the interfacial transfer and the surrounding combustion characteristics. Front caps enhance local evaporation near the junction between the cap and the aluminum body, whereas heat absorption by rear caps contributes to lower reaction temperatures. Variations in integrated heat release generally follow those in the evaporation rate. Based on the simulation results, the Lagrangian modeling framework was first revised for spherical particles. The film state is approximated using a 0.55-rule applied to temperature, species mass fractions, and pressure, from which the remaining thermophysical properties are derived. A simplified composition scheme enables film-state viscosity and fuel diffusivity to be pre-calculated as functions of temperature. Optimized Whitaker and Schiller-Naumann correlations were developed for the mass evaporation rate and drag force coefficient, respectively, showing good agreement with the simulation results. The framework was further extended to doublet particles with oxide caps. Accounting for the exposed aluminum area provides good evaporation predictions for rear caps, while front caps require a correction to the surface-averaged evaporation mass flux, particularly at high $\mathrm{Re_p}$.

infographic.key_insight: Oxide-cap position alters aluminum-particle combustion: front caps enhance local evaporation near the cap–metal junction, while rear caps absorb heat and lower reaction temperatures.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Cap-aware evaporation and drag models can improve Lagrangian predictions of burning aluminum particles without resolving each particle’s boundary layer.
method: Boundary-layer resolved simulations varying cap size, cap orientation, and particle Reynolds number.
Revised spherical-particle modeling using a 0.55-rule for film-state properties and optimized evaporation and drag correlations.
Extended modeling to capped doublet particles using exposed aluminum area and a front-cap evaporation correction.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports good agreement between optimized correlations and simulations, with integrated heat release generally tracking evaporation rate, but provides no numerical error metrics.
infographic.watch_item: Exposed-area scaling alone is insufficient for front caps, particularly at high particle Reynolds numbers, where evaporation-flux corrections are needed.
infographic.paper_title: Influence of an oxide cap on the combustion of aluminum particles using boundary-layer resolved simulations

title: Partitioned iterative FD-SPH for fluid-rigid-body interaction: Stability and validation for lightweight floating bodies
authors: Kumpei Tsuji, Ciara Galvin, Hiroyuki Omura, Naoto Mitsume, Mitsuteru Asai
abstract: This study assesses partitioned iterative fictitious-domain smoothed particle hydrodynamics (FD-SPH) for free-surface fluid-rigid-body interaction. Extending a strong-coupling framework for deformable structures, it combines volume-based hydrodynamic loads with Newton-Euler rigid-body updates. Within each time step, the mismatch between pressure-projected fictitious-fluid and rigid-body velocities is fed back iteratively. A fractional-step interpretation identifies conditions under which Passively Moving Solid (PMS) projection and Newton-Euler updates yield identical rigid-body velocities. Single-pass and iterative FD-SPH are compared under matched conditions. A two-dimensional settling-disk benchmark agrees with published results. In three-dimensional buoyancy-driven cube tests, single-pass coupling becomes unstable at specific gravities of 0.1 and 0.2. At 0.1, reducing the time-step size by a factor of 500 does not suppress the instability. Iterative strong coupling remains stable across the tested range of 0.1-1.0. Equilibrium heights and orientations agree with hydrostatic expectations and published stable configurations, respectively. Two- and three-dimensional wet-bed dam-break simulations reproduce experimental trends in wave elevation and floating-body heave and pitch. Two star-shaped rigid bodies demonstrate applicability to complex geometries without explicit interface reconstruction or surface-normal evaluation. All production strong-coupling simulations satisfy the prescribed relative-residual criterion at every time step before reaching the maximum coupling-iteration count. These results support iterative FD-SPH for lightweight and complex floating bodies in transient free-surface flows.

infographic.key_insight: Iterative strong coupling stabilizes FD-SPH simulations of lightweight floating rigid bodies where single-pass coupling fails, even with drastic time-step reduction.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach supports simulation of lightweight and complex floating bodies in transient free-surface flows without explicit interface reconstruction or surface-normal evaluation.
method: Combine volume-based hydrodynamic loads with Newton–Euler rigid-body updates.
Iteratively correct the velocity mismatch between pressure-projected fictitious fluid and rigid bodies within each time step.
Use a fractional-step interpretation to identify conditions for equivalent PMS projection and Newton–Euler velocities.
infographic.evidence_signal: Iterative coupling remained stable for tested cube specific gravities of 0.1–1.0, while settling-disk and dam-break benchmarks agreed with published results and experimental trends.
infographic.watch_item: Strong coupling requires repeated updates within each time step; all production runs met the residual criterion, but the abstract does not quantify computational overhead.
infographic.paper_title: Partitioned iterative FD-SPH for fluid-rigid-body interaction: Stability and validation for lightweight floating bodies

title: Scattering by Small Ice Crystals in Turbulence: From Orientation Statistics to Retrieval Biases
authors: Himanshu Mishra, Mohd. Meraj Khan, T. Narayana Rao, Anubhab Roy
abstract: Ice-cloud retrievals from polarimetric radar, lidar and submillimeter radiometry commonly assume random orientation, horizontal alignment or a prescribed flutter angle. We link the orientation dynamics of ice crystals to their scattering. Fluid-inertial torque turns small settling crystals broadside on, and turbulent velocity gradients turn them away, so their orientation depends on the dissipation rate. We combine a closed-form orientation distribution for overdamped spheroids, including rotational diffusion and turbulence intermittency, with orientation-averaged Rayleigh, Rayleigh--Gans, T-matrix and specular scattering. Turbulence enters the scattering only through the Legendre moments of the orientation distribution. In the Rayleigh regime the specific differential phase follows crystal alignment, so assuming perfectly horizontal crystals biases ice-water-content retrievals low. Combining the specific differential phase with differential reflectivity limits this bias to $25\%$ for a single size of the shapes studied. For size distributions that span the alignment transition the bound can fail, because the two observables weight sizes differently. Depolarization adds sensitivity to higher-order moments and to intermittency. At finite size the second orientation moment mainly controls the scattering cross sections and the asymmetry parameter, and for optically soft crystals its contribution vanishes $54.7^\circ$ from the vertical. Specular returns from partly aligned plates should persist for lidars pointed $3^\circ$ from nadir. An exploratory analysis of EarthCARE lidar data finds a weakly depolarizing, low-lidar-ratio signature most frequent near $-11^\circ$C, where plates grow. Degree-scale tilt widths inferred from glints and lidar require larger crystals, near or beyond the validity range of the model.

infographic.key_insight: Turbulence changes ice-crystal alignment and scattering, so assuming perfectly horizontal crystals can underestimate ice-water content.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Orientation-aware scattering models can help reduce biases in polarimetric radar, lidar and submillimeter ice-cloud retrievals.
method: Model overdamped spheroid orientations using settling-induced torque, turbulent gradients, rotational diffusion and intermittency.
Couple orientation statistics to Rayleigh, Rayleigh–Gans, T-matrix and specular scattering through Legendre moments.
Assess retrieval biases and compare predicted lidar signatures with exploratory EarthCARE observations.
infographic.evidence_signal: Combining specific differential phase with differential reflectivity limits bias to 25% for single-size populations of the studied shapes; exploratory EarthCARE data show the predicted lidar signature most often near −11°C.
infographic.watch_item: The 25% bound can fail for size distributions spanning the alignment transition, and degree-scale tilt widths require crystals near or beyond the model’s validity range.
infographic.paper_title: Scattering by Small Ice Crystals in Turbulence: From Orientation Statistics to Retrieval Biases

title: Effective-dimension estimation of a minimal turbulent channel flow via IRMAE-WD
authors: Ryuto Saeki, Keita Nakamura, Koji Fukagata
abstract: The implicit rank-minimizing autoencoder with weight decay (IRMAE-WD) (Zeng et al. 2024) aims to estimate the dimension of the low-dimensional manifold underlying high-dimensional data from a sharp drop in the latent singular values of a single trained model. We apply IRMAE-WD with a three-dimensional convolutional autoencoder to velocity fields of a minimal turbulent channel flow at ${\rm Re}_τ=110$ and examine whether the drop represents the intrinsic degrees of freedom. We also compare the number of coordinates IRMAE-WD needs for a given reconstruction accuracy or smallest reproduced scale with that of proper orthogonal decomposition (POD). We find that a clear drop appears and that the reconstruction rate decreases by at most 0.01 percentage points with truncation at the drop. The drop thus marks the effective dimension of the trained representation. However, the drop position moves to the lower-dimension side as linear layers are added. In addition, the reconstruction error decreases only gradually with the number of coordinates in all but the smallest wavelength band. These results suggest that the drop position is set by the implicit regularization of the linear layers and cannot be regarded as the intrinsic degrees of freedom. In contrast, with transfer learning, the smallest number of coordinates needed for a given accuracy hardly depends on the number of linear layers and is smaller than that of POD up to a reconstruction rate of about 97%. IRMAE-WD also reproduces a given scale with fewer coordinates than POD. Above about 97%, however, POD requires fewer coordinates, mainly because IRMAE-WD reconstructs large-scale structures less precisely. Hence, when the error decreases continuously, as in the minimal channel flow, the number of coordinates needed to represent wall turbulence should be stated with the required accuracy or scale, not as a single number.

infographic.key_insight: IRMAE-WD’s latent singular-value drop marks the effective dimension of its trained representation, not necessarily the intrinsic degrees of freedom of turbulence.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Compact representations of wall turbulence should be selected for a required reconstruction accuracy or resolved scale, rather than a single dimension estimate.
method: Apply IRMAE-WD with a 3D convolutional autoencoder to minimal-channel velocity fields at Reτ = 110.
Vary the number of linear layers and truncate latent coordinates at the singular-value drop.
Use transfer learning to compare coordinate requirements against POD by reconstruction accuracy and reproduced scale.
infographic.evidence_signal: Truncation at the drop reduced reconstruction rate by at most 0.01 percentage points; with transfer learning, IRMAE-WD needed fewer coordinates than POD up to about 97% reconstruction, while POD was more compact above that level.
infographic.watch_item: The drop shifts toward fewer dimensions as linear layers are added, so it should not be treated as an architecture-independent measure of intrinsic flow dimension.
infographic.paper_title: Effective-dimension estimation of a minimal turbulent channel flow via IRMAE-WD
